intro: Adverbs of manner say how you do something: slowly, well, carefully. Most of them are formed with -ly (slow → slowly). But some very common ones are irregular (good → well, fast, hard), and their position in the sentence follows strict rules.
objectifs: Form an -ly adverb from an adjective, with the spelling rules.
Know the irregular adverbs: well, fast, hard, late, early, and the false friends hardly and lately.
Put the adverb in the right place: after the verb and its object, never between them.
Choose between an adjective and an adverb, especially after look, feel, sound, smell, taste.

texte: An adjective describes a noun (a slow car, she is careful). An adverb of manner describes a verb: the way someone does the action (the car moves slowly, she drives carefully).
Compare: He's a careful driver (adjective, before the noun driver) / He drives carefully (adverb, after the verb drives). Both sentences have the same meaning.
exemples: She's a quiet person. She speaks quietly.
The test was easy. I passed it easily.
He's a bad singer. He sings badly.

texte: Usually, add -ly to the adjective: slow → slowly, careful → carefully (double l, because careful already ends in l), quick → quickly.

lignes: quick → quickly, bad → badly, careful → carefully, polite → politely
easy → easily, happy → happily, angry → angrily
gentle → gently, simple → simply, possible → possibly, terrible → terribly
fantastic → fantastically, automatic → automatically (exception: public → publicly)

texte: The adverb of “good” is “well”: She's a good cook. She cooks well. This is the most common irregular adverb, and the one learners forget most.

Some adverbs have the same form as the adjective: fast (a fast car / he drives fast), hard (hard work / she works hard), late (a late train / I arrived late), early (an early flight / we left early), straight (go straight on). Never say “fastly”.
Be careful: “hardly” and “lately” exist, but with a DIFFERENT meaning. Hardly = almost not (I can hardly hear you). Lately = recently (I've been tired lately).
exemples: She works hard, but she hardly sleeps.
sections.note: Adjectives that already end in -ly (friendly, lovely, lonely, silly, ugly) have no adverb. Say “in a friendly way”: She smiled in a friendly way.

texte: An adverb of manner goes after the verb, or after the object if there is one. Golden rule: NEVER put it between the verb and its object. Say: He speaks English well (not “He speaks well English”).
For emphasis, some adverbs can go before the verb: She quickly closed the door. But “well” and the adverbs with the same form as the adjective (fast, hard) always go after.

After be, look, feel, sound, smell, taste, seem, become and get, use an ADJECTIVE, not an adverb: you describe the subject, not an action. You look tired. This soup tastes good. The idea sounds great.
Compare: She looks happy (her appearance: adjective) / She looked at me happily (the action of looking: adverb).
Special case: “well” can be an adjective meaning “healthy”: I don't feel well (I feel ill). “I feel good” means I feel happy, in good form.
exemples: Are you OK? You don't look well.

formule: adjective + ly → adverb (slowly, carefully, easily, gently) · good → well · fast, hard, late, early = same form · verb + object + adverb
prononciation: The -ly ending is weak: /li/. The stress stays on the same syllable as the adjective: CAREful → CAREfully /ˈkeəfəli/.
“-ically”: you often hear only /ɪkli/ at the end: fantastically /fænˈtæstɪkli/.
“well” /wel/: one vowel sound, as in “bell”, with a clear l at the end.
“hardly” /ˈhɑːdli/: don't confuse it with “hard” when you speak; -ly changes the whole meaning.
erreurs: Don't separate the verb and its object.
The adverb of good is well.
Fast is the same as an adjective and an adverb.
Hard = with effort; hardly = almost not.
She answered in a friendly way.
Friendly is an adjective; it has no -ly adverb.

dialogue.contexte: After a driving lesson in Namur, an instructor talks to her student.
lignes: Well done, Kevin. You drove very carefully today.
Thanks! But I parked the car badly, didn't I?
A little. You need to turn the wheel more slowly. And you sometimes brake too hard.
I know. I get nervous when cars drive fast behind me.
That's normal. Just breathe deeply and stay calm.
Do you think I'm ready for the test?
Almost. You learn quickly and you listen well. Two more lessons, and you'll pass easily.
That sounds great! See you on Thursday.

mots: Drive carefully. The road is wet.
with attention, to avoid mistakes or danger
Can you speak more slowly, please?
You can easily find the station.

exercices.consigne: Write the adverb of the adjective.
Rewrite the sentence with the verb in brackets and an adverb.
items: My brother is a fast runner. (run)

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Correct it.
items: You did the exercise very good.
You did the exercise very well.
Please drive slow in the village.
Please drive slowly in the village.

exercices.consigne: Complete with the right adverb or adjective from the word in brackets.
items: Speak more ___, please. I don't understand. (slow)
I can ___ hear you. The music is too loud. (hard)

exercices.consigne: Write five sentences about how you (or people you know) do things: speak a language, cook, drive, work, sleep. Use at least one irregular adverb (well, fast, hard).
items: I speak French fluently and English quite well. My father cooks badly, but he cleans the kitchen carefully. My sister drives too fast. I usually work hard on Mondays. On Sundays I sleep late and wake up slowly.

a_retenir: Adjective + ly → adverb; easy → easily, gentle → gently, fantastic → fantastically.
good → well; fast, hard, late, early: same form. hardly = almost not, lately = recently.
Position: verb + object + adverb (She speaks English well).
After be, look, feel, sound, smell, taste, seem: adjective (You look tired).
friendly, lovely, lonely are adjectives: in a friendly way.
